items.note: Bhoja as scholar of many subjects (grammar, literature, drama, music, water management, vastu, town planning, temple building) with a famed council of scholars.
items.gloss: Bhoja was not just a king; he was also a deep scholar of many subjects. There was a famous council of scholars of grammar, language, literature, drama, dance, music, water management, vastu, town planning, temple building and architecture, which scholars even from Kashmir competed to join.

items.note: Bhoja's buildings were called Sarasvati Kanthabharana, the title of two books he wrote and his own epithet.
items.gloss: In Bhoja's time their names were Sarasvati Kanthabharana. He wrote two books of this name, and it was also his title.

items.note: In 1401 Dilawar Khan Ghuri converted Bhoja-era sites at Ujjain, Dhar and Mandu in the same way (pattern of conversion of Paramara buildings).
items.gloss: In 1401 Dilawar Khan Ghuri turned these splendid Bhoja-era places at Ujjain, Dhar and Mandu all at once into similar stupa-covered structures. Enclosed complexes were built from the rubble of the Sarasvati Kanthabharana, now called Bhojshala. In Ujjain it is today a mosque without foundation in Anantpeth locality.

items.note: Author names Mahlakdeva as last Paramara king, in whose time Iltutmish raided Malwa and temples were razed; Minhaj Siraj and Ibn Battuta cited as witnesses.
items.gloss: The last Paramara king is Mahlakdeva, in whose time Delhi's raider Shamsuddin Iltutmish attacked Malwa. All the temples of the area were razed. The Mahakal temple in Ujjain was looted and broken for the first time then. Iltutmish carried the images of Mahakal and Vikramaditya to Delhi and had them thrown outside a mosque. Minhaj Siraj bears witness; Ibn Battuta saw those images lying outside the mosque in Delhi.

items.note: Dilawar Khan Ghuri as first independent sultan of Malwa about 125 years before Babur; Hoshang Shah Ghuri broke Bhoja's dam near Bhojpur.
items.gloss: Dilawar Khan Ghuri became the first independent sultan of Malwa, a century and a quarter before Babur came to India. Hoshang Shah Ghuri was his successor, after whom Hoshangabad is named, and who had Bhoja's dam near Bhojpur in Bhopal broken.

items.note: Author's assessment of Bhoja's legacy: fostered arts, honoured the talented, built, wrote books, founded Sarasvati Kanthabharana centres of learning.
items.gloss: Like an ideal ruler Bhoja developed all kinds of arts in his kingdom. He gave honourable place around him to people of merit. He had splendid buildings made. He wrote books. He established centres of knowledge like Sarasvati Kanthabharana to shape the new generation.

items.note: Lane to the temple cleared ten feet each side; shopkeepers rebuilding; one house bearing a Jama Masjid signboard still projected into the road.
items.gloss: In the narrow lane ten feet on each side had been cleared. Those whose house and shop fronts were removed were starting to rebuild. But on the left stood the house projecting into the road on which we had seen a Jama Masjid signboard. Its ten-foot portion alone had not been touched.

items.note: Malluchand Jain's house next to the temple lane: temple fragments everywhere and inner rooms like a sanctum with carved sculptural stones, possible room below the floor.
items.gloss: Broken remains of the temple were visible everywhere in and outside his house. The rooms inside looked ten centuries old, like a temple sanctum set with carved stones of splendid sculptures. There was no image inside but two more rooms nearby; very old construction. The stones of the floor of the dark left room sounded as if another room lay beneath.

items.note: Only three Jain families remain in Udaypur.
items.gloss: Malluchandji told us that only three Jain families are left in Udaipur.

items.note: Jain's house was once buried in a mound; clearing for living space revealed rooms of finely carved stone, filled with junk sold to a scrap dealer.
items.gloss: This house was once buried in a mound. They lived in the front part. When clearing the mound began for more living space, rooms built of splendidly carved stones were found. They were filled with a lot of junk, which was sold to a scrap dealer.

items.note: A wooden top of a sitar or sarangi survived in the buried room's junk.
items.gloss: Praveen Sharma brought from inside a piece of an old musical instrument. It was the wooden top of a sitar or sarangi that had survived in the junk of the room buried in the mound.

items.note: Author infers from the instrument that music teaching or musicians existed here, a troupe for Shiva hymns at the temple (inference).
items.gloss: Finding a musical instrument at least told that there must have been teaching of music or music experts here. Certainly a group of musicians must have been here for the hymns to Shiva sung in the temple.

items.note: Paramara kings were learned patrons with experts in language, grammar, poetry, drama, architecture, astrology and music around them; Udayaditya's upbringing presumed similar.
items.gloss: One reason for the repute of the art-loving Paramara kings was that they were great lovers of learning. Experts in language, grammar, poetry, drama, vastu, architecture, astrology and music were around them. Raja Bhoj himself was a scholar among these talents. The environment around Udayaditya, brought up in such an atmosphere, must have been the same.

items.note: Old stepwell near a brick kiln with surprising design, spiral stone steps, and an inscription.
items.gloss: They took us to an old stepwell near a brick kiln whose design is astonishing. One could go down by strong spiral stone steps. There too we saw an inscription.

items.note: Carved stones from a collapsed building in a mound; an adjacent old ruin painted as a dargah.
items.gloss: Nearby, carved stones peeped out of bushes and rubble in a mound. It must have been a building that fell in a heap. Adjacent to it an old ruin had been painted and plastered as a dargah.

items.note: Paramara rulers Shiva worshippers; Udaypur on the Bundelkhand border was one of their busiest commercial centres.
items.gloss: The Paramara rulers were Shiva worshippers and in their reign of three-four hundred years built countless temples, schools and hostels in their vast kingdom. On the Bundelkhand border Udaipur was one of their busiest commercial centres, a fort-ringed town.

items.note: Fort-ringed town with a palace, several stepwells, gates, temples, squares and a court built over centuries; layout visible on Google Maps up to hill fortification.
items.gloss: In the fort-ringed town a palace, many stepwells, gates, temples, chowks and platforms, and a kachahari were built over centuries. The whole town plan can still be seen and understood on Google Map, extending to the fortification up to the hill.

items.note: Sequence of attacks (Iltutmish, Alauddin Khilji, Tughlaq, Sher Shah Suri); after Babur's 1528 attack on Chanderi, Udaypur became part of Chanderi suba.
items.gloss: In this area the attacks, plunder and occupation of Shamsuddin Iltutmish, Alauddin Khilji, Muhammad Tughlaq and Sher Shah Suri come in order. After the Mughals come new occupiers under the name of nawabs. Babur's attack on Chanderi was in 1528, and Udaipur, till then silently watching, became part of Chanderi suba.

items.note: Neighbours outside the temple (Raja Miyan, Hamid, Bashir, Ramesh, Praveen, Rajkumar) described as descendants of those who built the monuments together a thousand years ago.
items.gloss: Outside the temple on the left of the lane is Raja Miyan's home, further on a Hamid, opposite a Bashir, in between Ramesh, Praveen, Rajkumar. The great ancestors of all of them together performed these amazing constructions a thousand years ago.

items.note: Worship places in vast complexes as developed centres of education, culture and art, nurtured by the state and society.
items.gloss: These worship places in vast complexes were in fact developed, busy centres of education, culture and art, where a cultured new generation was shaped in the presence of the gods. The state nurtured them. Society preserved them.

items.note: A family's home is an old dwelling with fine carved art that had lain buried in an excavation and was cleaned with devotion; now their home.
items.gloss: An old dwelling with splendid artwork lay buried decades ago in the excavation. It was cleaned with devotion and effort. That is now their home, a lit page of the Udaipur tale.

items.note: A resident vacated extra space of his own accord, without any order, for Udaypur's good.
items.gloss: Happily he told that he had vacated more of his space, without any order. This earned merit of his share is for Udaipur's good.

items.note: Dr Mishra retrieved Udaypur inscriptions from the ASI archive whose English translation had been made long before.
items.gloss: He brought out from the archives of the Archaeological Survey of India some inscriptions that were of Udaipur and whose English translation had been made long ago.

items.note: Author notes the temple complex displays no Hindi translation of the Sanskrit inscriptions.
items.gloss: Why has no pure Hindi translation of the Sanskrit-origin inscriptions been displayed in the temple's vast complex?

items.note: INTACH (Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage) learned of the Udaypur efforts; Dr Madanmohan Upadhyay is its Bhopal convener.
items.gloss: One day news of our modest efforts in Udaipur reached INTACH, a capable non-governmental organisation that preserves archaeological monuments. Its Bhopal convener is Dr Madanmohan Upadhyay, a retired IAS officer.

items.note: INTACH Bhopal agreed to host a presentation on Udaypur on 2 March at the Tribal Museum hall.
items.gloss: When we narrated the experience of the Udaipur heritage walk, Upadhyayji was ready to hold our PowerPoint presentation on the Udaipur story in Bhopal next Sunday. This was a fresh offer from INTACH for Udaipur. I asked for 2 March; from that meeting the hall at the Tribal Museum on Shyamla Hills was booked.

items.note: Some visitors and officials had been to Udaypur but knew it only as the site of an ancient grand temple.
items.gloss: Some, who had gone to Udaipur at some time, knew Udaipur only by the temple: that an ancient grand temple is there.
